E.4.4 Unimodular Teleparallel Gravity The unimodular formulation has also been applied in the context of bouncing cosmologies. The Starobinsky inflation model [16, 1107, 1108, 1109] can be described via the Hubble evolution H(t) = Hi − M2 (t−ti) 6 , where ti is the time when inflation starts, Hi = H(t = ti) and M  1, and corresponds to the scale factor a(t) ∝ e Hi(t−ti)− 1 12M2 (t−ti) 2 . At early-times, a(t) ≈ e Hi(t−ti)− 1 6M2 tti . However, the ti 2 contribution is retained in Ref. [250], a(t) ≈ e Hi(t−ti)− 1 6M2 tti+ 1 2M2 ti 2 . (E.15) Transforming in terms of unimodular time coordinates, t 0 , leads to a(t 0 ) ∝ (t 0 − k) 1 3 , for some integration constant k, resulting in the singular unimodular Hubble parameter H = 1 3(t 0−k) 36 . Interestingly, T becomes constant making the Friedmann equation to become algebraic. Thus, a vast class of unimodular f(T) functions can host the singular bounce. Within the context of a unimodular boundary term fixing B(t 0 ) = −4Λ sets a(t 0 ) = aB[β(t 0 − tB 0 ) 2 + 1] 1 6 , where aB ≡ a(tB 0 ), β = Λ aB 6 which describes a cosmological sequence which passes through Type IV bounces, an inflationary phase and a standard decelerated cosmology. Despite no pathologies arise near the bounces, the cosmology ends in a Minkowskian fate making it a non-viable scenario [422] . Here, the associated reconstructed unimodular f(T) function expressed in terms of time is f(t 0 ) = − t 0 p βt02 + 1 ˆ λ(t 0 ) t 02 p βt02 + 1 dt 0 + p 2ρm,B βt02 + 1 2F1  − 1 2 , 1 + w 2 , 1 2 , −βt02  , (E.16) where λ(t 0 ) is the unimodular Lagrange multiplier and ρm,B ≡ ρm(tB 0 ). E.4.5 Perspectives on bouncing cosmologies in teleparallel cosmology The bouncing cosmological description aims to provide an alternative viewpoint to the beginning and late phases of the Universe. In the context of TG theories, bouncing cosmological scenarios can be generated either through a specification of the gravitational Lagrangian or via reconstruction methods. Thus, these bouncing cosmologies can be achieved without invoking any exotic matter. For instance, f(T) gravity can host a vast number of bouncing solutions with the possibility of realizing a suitable cosmological sequence, such as the Pseudo-Bang cosmology. Meanwhile, current 36The listed result differs quite considerably from that found in Ref. [250]. While a(t 0 ) differs from the one listed in Eq. (55), it agrees with Ref. [1109] even if the ti 2 contribution is included. 284 observations do not lead to the formation of a Type III singularity in the case of teleparallel DE whereas avoidance of ghost instabilities have been verified in f(T) gravity models. Meanwhile, f(T, B) gravity can also host a diverse number of bouncing solutions which Lagrangian is able to host vacuum (such as Minkowski) solutions, and can also generate the necessary accelerating contraction prior a Big Crunch. On the other hand, f(T, TG) gravity can be used to generate bouncing cosmologies, however, only the models hosting a Type III singularity were found to be compatible with the vacuum constraint. Finally, while the unimodular formulation can host the singular bounce, the theory has not yet been investigated in detail whether it can host other bouncing cosmologies. It is worth nothing that most of the reported analysis has been conducted within the aspect of reconstruction. An exception lies within f(T) gravity where the use of dynamical systems (some are also reported in Sec. 6.1.3) and its consequences in scalar and tensor power spectra (see Sec. 6.7.2) has been explored. While there has been works which briefly outline the existence of bouncing scenarios in other TG formulations (see Secs. 6.3.3, 6.5.3.1 and 6.6.4), there has not yet been an extensive analysis investigating the existence and suitable conditions to realise a viable cosmological bounce. More work has yet to be conducted in this sector. E.5 Anisotropic cosmologies in teleparallel theories of gravity In the previous sections, the Universe was assumed to be spatially homogeneous and isotropic leading to the extensive use of the FLRW metric. However, it is known that inhomogeneities and anisotropies do exist in the Universe, making the FLRW metric insufficient to describe these behaviors unless inhomogeneous and anisotropic effects are included. As discussed in Sec. 7, these can be accounted for through small, linear perturbations in the FLRW metric. However, the cosmological perturbation procedure also has limitations, for instance when the size of the perturbations are comparable to the background cosmology. There are also other philosophical arguments to consider. Could the early Universe be initially anisotropic and inhomogeneous which isotropizes and homogenesizes at later times? If inflation did not occur, what other mechanism could have taken place which generated the anisotropies and inhomogeneities? Even though it has been observed that the CMB is statistically isotropic and Gaussian [1110], anomalies appear at large scales including: (i) a lack of power at largest scales (quadropole contributions), (ii) hemispherical asymmetry and (iii) a preferred alignment at largest scales (quadropole and octopole). These features, which appeared in both WMAP [1111, 1112, 1113, 1114, 1115, 1116] and Planck data [1117, 516], could indicate a departure from this statistical isotropy principle. While investigations whether these are sourced from possible systematics in the experiments (WMAP [1111, 1116], Planck [516]), a deviation from statistical isotropy may still be a reality. A possible resolution is through the use of Bianchi models [1118, 1119], metrics which are spatially homogeneous but not necessarily isotropic. In this way, these could describe an initial anisotropic cosmology which correctly accounts for the early Universe anisotropies while it isotropizes at latetimes leading to the overall observed FLRW cosmology. While a brief overview of the Bianchi metrics is provided, a detailed account is available in Refs. [1120, 1121, 1122, 1123]. Given a set of spatial basis vectors ei obeying the relations [ei , ej ] = C k ijek , (E.17) where [·, ·] is the commutator and C k ij are structure constants, their associated dual vectors wk are constructed through dw k = − 1 2 C k ijw i ∧ w j , (E.18) where ∧ represents the exterior product. This leads to the construction of the Bianchi metric ds 2 = dt 2 − γij (t)w iw j , (E.19) 285 where γij is the spatial metric. Nine distinct types of Bianchi models, referred to as Type I–IX (BT-I–BT-IX), can be constructed from the structure constants, which are further classified under two classes: 1. Class A: BT-I, II, VI0, VII0, VIII, IX; 2. Class B: BT-III, IV, V, VIh and VIIh. The parameter h is an arbitrary non-zero parameter which generates a family of isometries for Types VI and VII. The Bianchi models have been extensively studied in the context of cosmology. In the case of the background evolution, Collins and Hawking have shown that for ordinary matter universes, most Bianchi models become anisotropic at early-times even if the Universe is very isotropic at late-times [1124]. Furthermore, Wald showed that for a positive cosmological constant, Bianchi universes become isotropic at late-times [1125]. Hu and Parker showed that for a renormalized energy-momentum tensor of a quantised matter field in a BT-I model, particle creation during times of the order of a Planck time could be strong enough to isotropize the Universe at an early-time [1126]. BT-III models have also been studied for late-time isotropy [1113]. In the case of CMB anisotropies, Class B models generate a spiral-pattern and hot spot regions, while BT-IX models can affect the quadropole spectrum [1120, 1127]. The quadropole effects can also be investigated through other Bianchi spacetimes [1113, 1111, 1115, 1128, 1129, 1114]. While cosmological perturbations are mainly considered for the FLRW cosmology, a similar approach can be considered for Bianchi metrics. As discussed in Refs. [1112, 1114], the approaches are distinct for non-perfect fluids and the perturbation equations become scale dependent, which introduce a coupling between the scalar and tensor modes leading to a scalar-tensor see-saw mechanism. E.5.1 Tetrad and spin connection in anisotropic cosmologies For every Bianchi model choice, an associated tetrad needs to be constructed such that it generates the Bianchi metric. However, as discussed in Sec. 5.12, this tetrad does not guarantee that it satisfies the field equations. Adequately, a good tetrad-spin connection pair must be considered to host a consistent set of field equations. In the following, we shall first present and discuss the diagonal tetrad with zero spin connection for the BT-I, BT-III, Kantowski-Sachs and Kasner metrics in the context of the f(T, B) gravity. For the BT-III case, this choice does not constitute a good tetrad-spin connection pair. Thus, we then present a novel set of good tetrad-spin connection pairs for a selection of Bianchi models which have not yet appeared in literature. E.5.1.1 Using a diagonal tetrad - not good tetrad-spin connection pair Based on the anisotropic cosmological models considered in teleparallel theories of gravity, only a select number of Bianchi type metrics shall be explored in detail, namely BT-I and III. Furthermore, Kantowski-Sachs [1130] and Kasner [1131] spacetimes are also discussed in f(T). The BT-III metric in Cartesian coordinates is given to be ds 2 = dt 2 − a 2 (t)dx 2 − e −2αxb 2 (t)dy 2 − c 2 (t)dz 2 , (E.20) where α is a constant parameter and a(t), b(t) and c(t) are the directional scale factors. Trivially, the FLRW metric is obtained when a = b = c and α = 0. On the other hand, BT-I is obtained when α = 0 while the locally rotationally symmetric BT-I and Kantowski-Sachs models are obtained when α = 0 and b = c. Lastly, the Kasner universe is obtained when α = 0 and the scale factors reduce to power-law behaviors a(t) ∝ t p1 , b(t) ∝ t p2 and c(t) ∝ t p3 with p1,2,3 are constants obeying the Kasner relations P 3 i=1 pi = 1, and P 3 i=1 pi 2 = 1. 286 Next, we choose a tetrad-spin connection pair which yields the metric. One natural choice that would generalize the flat FLRW tetrad (6.4) is the diagonal tetrad e A µ = diag 1, a(t), e−αxb(t), c(t) , (E.21) and zero spin connection components, for which the torsion scalar and the boundary term become T = −2 (HaHb + HaHc + HbHc) , (E.22a) B = 2α 2 a 2 − 2 h H˙ a + H˙ b + H˙ c + (Ha + Hb + Hc) 2 i , (E.22b) where Ha = ˙a/a, Hb = ˙b/b, Hc = ˙c/c represent the directional Hubble parameters. Finally, it is convenient to define an average Hubble parameter H ≡ 1 3 (Ha + Hb + Hc) , (E.23) which describes the average expansion of this universe. Consequently, an average scale factor a˜ ≡ (abc) 1/3 is defined. Naturally, this is related to the average Hubble parameter through the standard relation H = a/˜˙ a˜. Interestingly, the effect of α is absent in the torsion scalar, which has important consequences to the field equations, which is best illustrated through the context of f(T, B) gravity. Assuming a perfect fluid with anisotropic pressures in each spatial direction, px,y,z, for this choice of tetrad, the field equations of f(T, B) gravity result into κ 2 ρ = − f 2 + fT  T + α 2 a 2  + BfB 2 + ˙fB (Ha + Hb + Hc) , (E.24a) −κ 2 px = − f 2 − fT h (Hb + Hc) 2 + Ha(Hb + Hc) + H˙ b + H˙ c i − (Hb + Hc) ˙fT + BfB 2 + ¨fB , (E.24b) −κ 2 py = − f 2 − fT h (Ha + Hc) 2 + Hb(Ha + Hc) + H˙ a + H˙ c i − (Ha + Hc) ˙fT + BfB 2 + ¨fB , (E.24c) −κ 2 pz = − f 2 − fT  (Hb + Ha) 2 + Hc(Hb + Ha) + H˙ b + H˙ a − α 2 a 2  − (Ha + Hb) ˙fT + BfB 2 + ¨fB , (E.24d) 0 = α (Ha − Hb) fT , (E.24e) and there is an additional equation from the antisymmetric part, namely 1 2 α( ˙fT + ˙fB) = 0 . (E.25) The respective f(T) field equations reported in Refs. [1132, 1133] are also recovered. The last (antisymmetric) equation shows the problem of the choice of the tetrad not being compatible with a zero spin connection, since the only way to solve it is either α = 0 (which recovers BT-I), or f = f(−T + B) which is just f( ◦ R), or T˙ = B˙ = 0. In the latter case, however, this reduces to ΛCDM. On the other hand, BT-I, Kantowski-Sachs, locally rotationally symmetric and Kasner cosmologies do not host this issue as the antisymmetric equation Eq. (E.25) is naturally satisfied. At least in the context of f(T) gravity, there has been an attempt to obtain a consistent set of field equations [1134]. However, it has been unsuccessful since an incompatible tetrad-spin connection pair was considered. A resolution of this issue is explored in the following part. E.5.1.2 Using a good tetrad-spin connection pair As we saw in the previous section, for BT-III, if one uses the diagonal tetrad in Eq. (E.21) in the Weitzenböck gauge, the antisymmetric field equations in f(T) gravity constrain the model to be TEGR (or to become BT-I). This is related to the choice of the tetrad-spin connection pair that is not compatible with the symmetries of the system. In this section, we will derive a good tetrad-spin 287 connection pair for f(T, B) gravity for different types of Bianchi models. Let us first start with the following metric ds 2 = dt 2 − σ1(t, x, y, z)dx 2 − σ2(t, x, y, z)dy 2 − σ3(t, x, y, z)dz 2 , (E.26) where σi are arbitrary functions of the Cartesian coordinates. This metric is in the form of BT-I, BT-III, BT-V and BT-VI. Let us then start by assuming a zero spin connection and start with following diagonal tetrad e A µ = diag(1, σ1, σ2, σ3), (E.27) which is not a good tetrad-spin connection pair choice. Then, we can perform a Lorentz transformations e 0A µ = ΛA Be B µ with the three Euler αi angles which explicitly gives us the following rotated tetrad e 00 = dt , (E.28a) e 01 = σ1 cos α2 cos α3 dx − σ2(sin α1 sin α2 cos α3 + cos α1 sin α3) dy + σ3(sin α1 sin α3 − cos α1 sin α2 cos α3) dz , (E.28b) e 02 = σ1 cos α2 sin α3 dx + σ2(cos α1 cos α3 − sin α1 sin α2 sin α3) dy − σ3(cos α1 sin α2 sin α3 + sin α1 cos α3) dz , (E.28c) e 03 = σ1 sin α2 dx + σ2 sin α1 cos α2 dy + σ3 cos α1 cos α2 dz , (E.28d) where αi can depend on all the coordinates (t, x, y, z). If we replace this tetrad into the f(T, B) gravitational field equations (5.80), we get that the antisymmetric equations become 0 = ( ˙fB + ˙fT ) h σ3 (σ1 (α2,y sin α1 + α3,y cos α1 cos α2) − σ2,x) + σ2 (σ1 (α2,z cos α1 − α3,z sin α1 cos α2) − σ3,x) i , (E.29a) 0 = ( ˙fB + ˙fT ) (σ1 (σ2 (α1,z + α3,z sin α2) − σ3,y) − σ3 (σ2 (α2,x sin α1 + α3,x cos α1 cos α2) + σ1,y)) , (E.29b) 0 = ( ˙fB + ˙fT ) (σ1 (σ3 (α1,y + α3,y sin α2) + σ2,z) + σ2 (σ3 (α2,x cos α1 − α3,x sin α1 cos α2) + σ1,z)) . (E.29c) Here, commas denote derivatives. Clearly if ˙fB + ˙fT 6= 0 (which is a theory different to f( ◦ R) gravity), the system is difficult to solve. It is also easy to see that if αi = 0, one cannot have a solution for the system for ˙fB + ˙fT 6= 0. Then, we need the functions αi in order to solve the antisymmetric equations and then to find a good tetrad-spin connection pair. Since the majority of Bianchi models with a diagonal metric form only depend on the time coordinate and only one extra Cartesian coordinate, we will concentrate on three specific types of metrics: 1. All metric functions depending on t and x: σ1 = σ1(t, x), σ2 = σ2(t, x) and σ3 = σ3(t, x) 2. All metric functions depending on t and y: σ1 = σ1(t, y), σ2 = σ2(t, y) and σ3 = σ3(t, y) 3. All metric functions depending on t and z: σ1 = σ1(t, z), σ2 = σ2(t, z) and σ3 = σ3(t, z) BT-I, BT-III and BT-V are subcases of 1. and BT-VI is a subcase of 3. For the three cases mentioned above, it is possible to solve the antisymmetric equations (E.29a)–(E.29c) by choosing Case 1: cos α1 = σ2,xσ3 + σ2σ3,x σ1σ2 , α2 = z , α3 = π 2 . (E.30a) Case 2: cos α2 = σ1,yσ3 + σ1σ3,y σ2σ3 , α3 = x , α1 = π . (E.30b) 288 Case 3: sin α2 = − σ1,zσ2 + σ1σ2,z σ1σ3 , α3 = y , α1 = π 2 . (E.30c) Using these results, we find that a good tetrad-spin connection pair for different Bianchi models with a zero spin connection, with the following tetrads: Bianchi Type I: ds 2 = dt 2 − a(t) 2 dx 2 − b(t) 2 dy 2 − c(t) 2 dz 2 , (E.31a) e 0A µ =   1 0 0 0 0 0 0 c 0 a cos z −b sin z 0 0 a sin z b cos z 0   . (E.31b) Bianchi Type II: ds 2 = dt 2 − a(t) 2 (dx − Kzdy) 2 − b(t) 2 dy 2 − c(t) 2 dz 2 , (E.31c) e 0A µ =   1 0 0 0 0 0 −b 0 0 a −Kza 0 0 0 0 c   . (E.31d) Bianchi Type III: ds 2 = dt 2 − a(t) 2 dx 2 − b(t) 2 e −2αx dy 2 − c(t) 2 dz 2 , (E.31e) e 0A µ =   1 0 0 0 0 0 αbc a e −αx c q 1 − α2c 2 a 2 0 a cos z −be−αx sin z q 1 − α2c 2 a 2 αc2 sin z a 0 a sin z be−αx cos z q 1 − α2c 2 a 2 − αc2 cos z a   . (E.31f) Bianchi Type V: ds 2 = dt 2 − a(t) 2 dx 2 − e −2mx b(t) 2 dy 2 + c(t) 2 dz 2  , (E.31g) e 0A µ =   1 0 0 0 0 0 2mbc a e −2mx ce−mxq 1 − 4m2c 2e−2mx a 2 0 a cos z −be−mx sin z q 1 − 4m2c 2e−2mx a 2 2mc2e−2mx sin z a 0 a sin z be−mx cos z q 1 − 4m2c 2e−2mx a 2 − 2mc2e−2mx cos z a   . (E.31h) Bianchi Type VI: ds 2 = dt 2 − a(t) 2 e −2mz dx 2 − b(t) 2 e 2nz dy 2 − c(t) 2 dz 2 , (E.31i) e 0A µ =   1 0 0 0 0 ae−mz cos y q c 2−b 2(m−n) 2e 2nz c 2 b 2 (n−m)e 2nz cos y c c sin y 0 ae−mz sin y q c 2−b 2(m−n) 2e 2nz c 2 b 2 (n−m)e 2nz sin y c −c cos y 0 ab(m−n)e z(n−m) c benzq c 2−b 2(m−n) 2e 2nz c 2 0   . (E.31j) 289 Bianchi Type IX: ds 2 = dt 2 − a(t) 2 (dx − cos y dz) 2 − b(t) 2 dy 2 + sin2 y dz 2  , (E.31k) e 0A µ =   1 0 0 0 0 0 −b cos x b sin x sin y 0 a 0 −a cos y 0 0 b sin x b cos x sin y   . (E.31l) Here, we have also used the same idea for other Bianchi models having cross terms in the metric. All of these tetrads are new results that have not been reported in the literature. It is also possible to make a Lorentz transformation to switch on the spin connection and rewrite the above tetrads in another way. It is important to mention that these good tetrad-spin connection pairs were found in f(T, B) gravity but, it can be shown that they are also good pairs for other more general modified teleparallel theories such as those with scalar fields f(T, B, φ, X) with φ = φ(t). Let us now re-derive the equations for the BT-III with the correct good tetrad-spin connection given by Eq. (E.31f) with a zero spin connection. For this spacetime the torsion scalar and the boundary term becomes T = − 2α 2 a 2 − 2(HaHb + HaHc + HbHc), (E.32a) B = −2 h H˙ a + H˙ b + H˙ c + (Ha + Hb + Hc) 2 i , (E.32b) where we clearly see that α now appears in T and does not appear in B. The cosmological equations then yield κ 2 ρ = − f 2 + fT  T + α 2 a 2  + BfB 2 + ˙fB (Ha + Hb + Hc) , (E.33a) −κ 2 px = − f 2 − fT  α 2 a 2 + (Hb + Hc) 2 + Ha(Hb + Hc) + H˙ b + H˙ c  − (Hb + Hc) ˙fT + BfB 2 + ¨fB , (E.33b) −κ 2 py = − f 2 − fT  α 2 a 2 + (Ha + Hc) 2 + Hb(Ha + Hc) + H˙ a + H˙ c  − (Ha + Hc) ˙fT + BfB 2 + ¨fB , (E.33c) −κ 2 pz = − f 2 − fT h (Hb + Ha) 2 + Hc(Hb + Ha) + H˙ b + H˙ a i − (Ha + Hb) ˙fT + BfB 2 + ¨fB , (E.33d) 0 = α (Ha − Hb) fT . (E.33e) We can notice a big difference between these field equations and the ones derived using the incorrect tetrad (E.24a)–(E.24e), which is that one does not have the antisymmetric equation (E.25). This equation is the one which constrains the model to be α = 0 or fT T = 0 (GR) or T˙ = 0 (GR again). Exactly as in GR (and TEGR), from Eq. (E.33e) one notices that one needs a fluid having a linear momentum with components T01 = T10 in order to construct a BT-III with Ha 6= Hb (or equivalently a 6= b). One interesting feature here is that for f = F(B) gravity (without having GR in the background), one can study BT-III with a 6= b for an anisotropic fluid without requiring to have a fluid with linear momentum. This feature cannot be achieved in GR. This explicit example related to BT-III shows that it is very important to be careful choosing the correct tetrad-spin connection pair when one is studying certain non-trivial geometries. It is important to mention that the vast majority of the literature related to anisotropic cosmology in TG did not consider this important point, and for this, many of them give incorrect conclusions about these models. As a future work, it would be interesting to re-analyze different Bianchi models using the correct tetrads shown here. E.5.2 Reconstruction method Reconstructing the gravitational Lagrangian in anisotropic universes has been vastly investigated in curvature-based theories [1135, 1136, 1137, 1138]. In contrast to the FLRW case, the reconstruction 290 approach is not straightforward due to an anisotropic metric and matter fluid, requiring further considerations and assumptions prior to solving for the unknown gravitational Lagrangian. Even if a cosmological evolution is assumed, one then has to consider whether this behavior is observed in particular directions or as an average expansion which may lead to distinguishable directional expansions. In what follows, various known cosmologies shall be examined in detail. E.5.2.1 de Sitter Spacetime In the first scenario, each individual direction is assumed to evolve following a de Sitter expansion behavior. However, each direction may not necessarily be expanding at the same rate, otherwise it reduces to the FLRW cosmology. This approach has been considered in Refs. [1132, 1139, 1140] using BT-I where the directional scale factors are taken to be in the form a(t) ∝ e Ha,0t , b(t) ∝ e Hb,0t , c(t) ∝ e Hc,0t , (E.34) where Ha,b,c,0 are constants. Note that the torsion scalar is now constant, T0. Assuming an isotropic fluid with constant EoS, the following scenarios are obtained: 1. w = −1: The fluid behaves as a cosmological constant leading to the condition κ 2 ρ = − f(T0) 2 + T0fT (T0), (E.35) where ρ is now constant in time. Choosing an f(T) function leads to an algebraic relation between Ha,b,c,0 which, however, constrains the geometry to reduce to the FLRW one. Alternatively, treating the equation as an ordinary differential equation gives the class of functions which naturally host the de Sitter behavior. The latter has been considered in Refs. [1139, 1140] where the matter fluid is assumed to behave as HDE, for which the f(T) Lagrangian reduces to a TEGR rescaling. 2. Ha,0 + Hb,0 + Hc,0 = 0: This implies that a decelerated expansion occurs along at least one spatial direction. The second scenario focuses on when the average Hubble parameter is a constant, H0. As investigated in Ref. [1141] for the locally rotationally symmetric BT-I cosmology (b = c), this assumption imposes the condition ab2 ∝ e 3H0t which is insufficient to reconstruct the Lagrangian. To this end, the anisotropic fluid is parametrized to behave as a cosmological constant at late-times through px = wxρ , py = pz = (wx + δ)ρ , (E.36) where δ is the skewness parameter and wx is chosen to be −1. In the special case of TEGR, an analytical form for the directional scale factors are obtained, a(t) ∝ e H0t  γ H0 + 3λe−3H0t − 2 3 , b(t) = e H0t  γ H0 + 3λe−3H0t 1 3 , (E.37) where γ, λ are integration constants. Consequently, the skewness parameter takes on the following form δ = − 27H0 2λ 2 e −3H0t γ (γe3H0t + 6H0λ) . (E.38) Evidently, this becomes a realistic model for a de Sitter late-time cosmology since, at late-times, A ' B and δ → 0, meaning this Universe becomes isotropized. From these considerations, the reconstruction method is then applied to obtain a functional form of the f(T) Lagrangian with the assumption that the directional scale factors take on the previously obtained forms Eq. (E.37). Careful re-examination of the work reveals that the continuity equation does not lead to the ordinary differential equation 1 + fT − fT T = 0 as reported in Ref. [1141], but reduces to an identity relation. In other words, the continuity equation is insufficient to constrain the Lagrangian. Further considerations of the fluid behavior, either through wx or δ, may be sufficient to reconstruct the f(T) function. 291 E.5.2.2 Power-law behavior Throughout the works in Refs. [1132, 1142, 1139, 1140, 1143], a power-law behavior has been considered for reconstruction. First, the standard power-law behavior a(t) ∝ t p1 , b(t) ∝ t p2 , c(t) ∝ t p3 , (E.39) where p1,2,3 are constants, is considered. This simple ansatz can host the Kasner metric provided that p1,2,3 obey the Kasner relations. However, the introduction of an arbitrary f(T) Lagrangian has important consequences to the existence of the Kasner metric or the form of the Kasner relations. Similar considerations appear in other modified theories of gravity [1144, 1145, 1146, 1147]. To illustrate this, starting from the torsion scalar, which is given to be T = −2t −2 (p1p2 + p1p3 + p2p3) , (E.40) is zero for a standard Kasner universe. In the absence of matter fluids, the Kasner cosmology is a solution to the field equations if f(0) = 0 provided that |fT (0)|, |fT T (0)| < ∞37. This allows for an extensive class of functions which can host the Kasner cosmology, including (i) power-law f(T) ∝ (−T) n for n > 0, and (ii) exponential f(T) = −T − T e−pT , p is some constant [1142, 1148]. Alternatively, a Kasner metric is obtained through the modification of Kasner’s relations [1142]. For instance, in the absence of matter fluids and taking f(T) ∝ (−T) n for n > 0, the field equations are satisfied if T = 0, which lead to the following modified Kasner relations: n > 0 : X 3 i=1 pi = 2n − 1 , X 3 i=1 pi 2 = (2n − 1)2 , (E.41a) n > 1 : X 3 i=1 pi = C0 , X 3 i=1 pi 2 = C0 2 , (E.41b) where C0 is some arbitrary constant. It can be observed that the standard Kasner universe is recovered only for n ≥ 1 by setting C0 = 1, while a non-standard one is obtained for 0 < n < 1. For non-Kasner cosmologies, a perfect isotropic fluid was considered in Refs. [1132, 1139, 1140, 1143] including constant EoS w, Ricci Dark Energy (RDE), New Agegraphic Dark Energy (NADE) and HDE (including their PLE corrections) fluid types. For the constant EoS case, the reconstructed Lagrangian is f(T) = 2κ 2ρ0 −1 + (1 + w)(p1 + p2 + p3)  −T 2χ n , χ ≡ p1p2 + p1p3 + p2p3 6= 0 . (E.42) Here, an expanding universe is obtained when χ < 0 which imposes the extra necessary condition (1 + w)β = 2n, n ∈ N, in order to maintain a real Lagrangian. Furthermore, the field equations give rise to two possible scenarios [1132]: 1. w(p1 + p2 + p3) = 1: Yields an anisotropic expansion within an isotropic fluid; 2. p1 = p2 = p3: Reduces to FLRW cosmology. For the remaining fluids, the reconstruction procedure was applied within an locally rotationally symmetric BT-I cosmology where the scale factors take on either standard power-law or pole-like forms satisfying38 a(t) = b(t) 1 m , with b(t) = b0(ts − t) mh , (E.43) 37A more general consideration can be taken, for example |fT (0)| → ∞ but |T fT |T→0 < ∞ but this has not been investigated in detail. 38The index h as seen in Refs. [1139, 1140] has been redefined in order to simplify the results. The original solutions are recovered via the transformation h → −h. In the case of Ref. [1143], the transformations h → −mh and m → 1/m need to be applied. 292 where b0, m, h are constants and ts ≥ t represents the time of a future singularity. For these cases, the f(T) Lagrangian was reconstructed and are summarized in Table 37. It is remarked that in Ref. [1139], the correct reconstructed solution is the pole-like one but the solution remains identical for the non-pole-like case. Furthermore, the solutions for PLECHDE and PLECNADE as given in Ref. [1143] are based on assuming the future event horizon and the conformal time computed based on the expansion of b(t) as opposed to the average scale factor. Overall, it is observed that the models reduce to power-law type models. The HDE and NADE reconstructed models derived in Ref. [1143] are recovered by setting β → 0. E.5.2.3 ΛCDM behavior The ΛCDM cosmology has been studied in Refs. [1149, 1150] for a perfect isotropic matter fluid with constant EoS w. Here, the cosmology is built on the principle that the average expansion is ΛCDM, meaning it obeys the same evolution equation H2 = H0 2 (Ωm0a˜ −3 + ΩΛ). However, since a˜ and H are now the average quantities, each spatial direction may now evolve differently from one another without each individually exhibiting a behavior similar to the ΛCDM cosmology. To reconstruct the Lagrangian, the matter fluid is expressed in terms of the torsion scalar as ρ = ρ0  J − T − 9H0 2ΩΛ 9H0 2Ωm0 1+w , (E.44) where ρ0 is some constant and J := Ha 2 + Hb 2 + Hc 2 . Then, using the Friedmann equations lead to the solution f(T) = √ −T ˆ−T 0 κ 2ρ0 x 3/2  J − x − 9H0 2ΩΛ 9H0 2Ωm0 1+w dx . (E.45) Here, the solution has been generalized for an arbitrary EoS. It is remarked that the signature of the fT coefficient of the Friedmann equation in Refs. [1149, 1150] is incorrect while the sin θ contributions in Ref. [1150] should not appear. Evidently, contrary to the FLRW case, an analytical expression cannot be obtained because J cannot be solely expressed in terms of T. Nonetheless, prior knowledge of the directional scale factors would resolve this issue. E.5.2.4 Unification of matter and dark energy behaviors The reconstruction for a unification of matter and DE domination epochs has been explored in Ref. [1132]. In particular, the model follows a similar approach to the one encountered in Ref. [457] but is now applied to the anisotropic BT-I cosmology. Here, each directional scale factor evolves as e hi(t) ln t where each hi(t) is a slowly varying function chosen to be hi(t) = hi,1 + hi,2ζt2 1 + ζt2 , (E.46) 293 where hi,1, hi,2 and ζ are positive constants. This choice signifies a directional decelerating era for 0 < hi < 1 and an accelerating era for hi > 1. Contrary to the FLRW case, however, the average expansion behavior of this universe may be different. This can be observed from the deceleration parameter q ∼ −1 + 3 hx + hy + hz ≡ −1 + 1 h˜ , (E.47) with h˜ representing the average of the slowly varying parameters. On average, deceleration is obtained when 0 < h <˜ 1 while acceleration for h >¯ 1, which implies that at least one spatial direction could have an opposite expansion behavior from the average one. Due to the complexity of the resulting field equations, an isotropic fluid as well a Kantowski-Sachs metric is assumed. As hi are slowly varying (h˙ i ∼ h¨ i ∼ 0), the reconstructed Lagrangian takes on the form39 f(T) ∝ exp  − 1 2 (1 + w)  ln (1 + ζΨ0(T)) (hx,2 + 2hy,2) + (hx,1 + 2hy,1) ln  Ψ0(T) 1 + ζΨ0(T)  , (E.48) where Ψ0(T) is the real root to the polynomial 0 = ζ 2TΨ0 3 + (2ζT + 2ζ 2X)Ψ0 2 + (T + 2ζZ)Ψ0 + 2Y , (E.49a) X ≡ hx,2hy,2 + hx,2hz,2 + hy,2hz,2, Y ≡ hx,1hy,1 + hx,1hz,1 + hy,1hz,1 , (E.49b) Z ≡ hx,1hy,2 + hx,2hy,1 + hx,1hz,2 + hx,2hz,1 + hy,1hz,2 + hy,2hz,1 . (E.49c) During early- and late-times, the Lagrangian takes on a more simplified form: At early-times: f(T) ∝ Ψ0(T) − 1+w 2 (hx,1+2hy,1) , (E.50a) At late-times: f(T) ∝ Ψ0(T) − 1+w 2 (hx,2+2hy,2) . (E.50b) Observe that at early-times, the reconstructed form depends on the constants hi,1 which highlight the early-time dominant behavior as seen from Eq. (E.46). Likewise, the late-time reconstructed form is dependent on hi,2 as expected. E.5.3 Noether’s symmetry approach The application of Noether symmetry for anisotropic cosmologies has been explored in curvaturebased theories. Searching for the existence of such symmetries allow for the simplification of the field equations while exploring the nature of the anisotropic cosmology, for instance, whether the latter isotropizes at late-times. Some works include, but are not limited to, Refs. [1151, 468, 1152, 1153, 1154, 1155]. In the context of TG, Refs. [1156, 1157, 1158] are reviewed. Starting with f(T) gravity, Ref. [1157] considers a Kantowski-Sachs spacetime in polar coordinates. However, the chosen diagonal tetrad e A µ = diag (1, a, b, b sin θ) proves to be problematic as the spin connection becomes non-zero which is not considered in the work. This is due the fact that the antisymmetric field equations were not checked for consistency. Thus, the resulting Noether symmetries and cosmologies may not be entirely correct. In Ref. [1156], a BT-I metric was considered with a configuration space Q = {t, a, b, c, T}. The Noether constraint imposes the functional Lagrangian to f(T) = −T + mT n for some constants m and n which, depending on the magnitude of n (n = 1 or n 6= 1), different Noether symmetries are obtained. However, it is remarked that Eq. (22) in Ref. [1156] is missing a factor of T for the fT T coefficients which may introduce more symmetries than those reported. While the resulting cosmology was not analyzed for n 6= 1, the directional scale factors have been solved for n = 1 (i.e. TEGR) when the matter fluid is absent. However, the scale factors do not host a simple analytic form and hence were not analyzed in detail. 39The solution obtained in Ref. [1132] is not recovered. 294 Besides, the anisotropic scenario, Ref. [1156] explores the FLRW limit where only a number of Noether symmetries remain. However, these do not match those investigated in Sec. 6.1.2 due to how the configuration space and the Noether condition are treated. When the FLRW limit is considered, the configuration space dimension Q decreases, adequately reducing the number of partial differential equations arising from the Noether condition. Thus, in order to correctly recover the system of equations, the FLRW limit must be taken before the Noether condition is considered. In fact, the partial differential equation [1156] c η1,a + b η4,a = 0 , (E.51) introduces the constraint a η ˜ 1,a˜ = 0, where a˜ now becomes the standard isotropic FLRW scale factor since a = b = c = ˜a. This extra constraint does not appear in the standard f(T) FLRW Noether equations. Next, TEGR in the presence of a scalar-electromagnetic field coupling is considered [1158] L = − T 2κ 2 − 1 2 φ,µφ ,µ + V (φ) + 1 4 f 2 (φ)FµνF µν . (E.52) As discussed in Sec. 6.5.2.1, due to the action’s equivalence with its curvature analogue, the same Noether symmetries are expected. An locally rotationally symmetric BT-I model (b = c) with a = b m for some constant m was then considered where the Noether condition constrains the potential and gauge kinetic functions to take the following forms: V (φ) ∝ c1e µφ − c2e −µφ2 , f(φ) ∝ c1e µφ − c2e −µφn , (E.53) where µ = m+2 2 √ 4m+2 and n = { 2−m 2+m , m 2+m } is a parameter which value depends on the choice of the electromagnetic vector potential. While a general cosmological behavior was not explored, four special cases were examined in detail: (i) c1 6= 0, c2 = 0, (ii) c1 = 0, c2 6= 0 and (iii) c1 = c2 = 1/2 (iv) c1 = −c2 = 1 2 . With appropriate fine-tuning of parameters, the resulting cosmology can match with observations and also in the last case some interesting potential forms arise that could account for a unified dark matter model. E.5.4 Cosmological stability and dynamical system approach In Refs. [1148, 1159], the background cosmological stability of a Kasner universe in the context of f(T) gravity was investigated in the case of vacuum. In Ref. [1159], a perturbative approach on the background Kasner cosmology was considered, which focuses on perturbing the directional scale factors A = {a, b, c} via A = A0 (1 + εAε) + O( 2 ), (E.54) where A0 ∝ (t p1 , tp2 , tp3 ) is the background Kasner cosmology, ε is an infinitesimal parameter and Aε = (aε, bε, cε) represent the directional scale factor perturbations. The stability is determined based on whether Aε grows or decays with time. On the other hand, a numerical integration on the field equations is performed in Ref. [1148] to investigate the stability of the Kasner cosmology. In both works, the power-law ansatz f(T) = −T − f0T n , where f0 is some constant and n ∈ N is considered while the exponential model f(T) = −T −f1 1 − e −pT m , where f1, p and m are constants is only considered in Ref. [1159]. Starting with the power-law case, as discussed in Sec. E.5.2, a Kasner solution only exists when T = 0 or T n−1 = 1 f0(1−2n) . The T = 0 case is an exact solution to the field equations and therefore stability is not considered. For the remaining case, at least for n ≥ 2, the Kasner solution is unstable and evolves towards a de Sitter attractor, which only exists when sign(f0) = (−1)n . While this unstable point is stated to be a saddle point in Ref. [1159], it actually represents a source in an expanding universe [1148]. For the exponential model case, the Kasner solution is a hyperbolic point (hence cannot be stable) for m = 1 while for m > 1, the behavior is identical to the power-law case discussed previously. However, the existence of de Sitter attractors it not explored for this case. 295 Meanwhile, the dynamical behavior of a BT-I cosmology has been investigated in Refs. [1159, 1160, 1161] for the f(T) = −T − f0T n ansatz. Starting with Ref. [1159] in the absence of matter fluids, for n = 2, the critical points (Ha ? , Hb ? , Hc ? ) P± = ±  1 6 √ f0 , 1 6 √ f0 , 1 6 √ f0  , P0 = (0, 0, 0) , (E.55) are obtained. P± correspond to a FLRW de Sitter cosmology while P0 represents a static universe. Furthermore, P− is unstable, P0 is a saddle point and P+ is stable, meaning that a BT-I cosmology can isotropize towards a de Sitter late-time behavior. While the full critical point analysis has not been explored for arbitrary n, a de Sitter attractor solution only exists when sign(f0) = (−1)n . In Ref. [1160], the effect of matter fluids is also considered. The chosen dimensionless phase-space variables are obtained by dividing Eq. (E.24a) with 9H2 fT to yield x˜ := T 9H2 , y˜ := f0(1 − 2n)T n−1 − 1 fT , r˜ := κ 2ρ 9H2fT . (E.56) As the dynamical variable r˜ appears in the Friedmann equations, it can be used to further constrain the parameter space leaving (˜x, y˜) as the free dynamical variables. This gives rise to a number of critical points, summarized in Table 38, which can be associated to distinct cosmological behaviors. [1160], which describe various cosmological scenarios. The nature of the critical points are also highlighted. Here, α = 1+w 1−w(n−1) and wcr. := 1 2n−1 have been defined. Evidently, the critical points describe both isotropic and anisotropic behaviors, and since certain isotropic critical points can be stable, isotropization of this universe can be achieved at late-times. Furthermore, the de Sitter isotropic solution is again recovered but, contrary to Ref. [1159], its stability is further emphasized by the EoS of the matter fluid. For the special cases n = 2, 3, the overall cosmological dynamical behavior has been analyzed in detail where, it has been observed that the behavior changes depending on the signature of f0. Starting with the n = 2 case: 1. f0 > 0: The universe starts at an anisotropic non-standard singularity where T finite but T˙ is divergent, which later isotropizes to either the power-law behavior (P3) or de Sitter (P4). 296 2. f0 < 0: A non-standard singularity where T approaches a point where fT = 0 is identified. The following scenarios are obtained: (a) Universe begins at either one of the critical points P1,2,5 which later evolves to the P3 behavior; (b) The Universe starts and finishes with the aforementioned non-standard singularity, which evolution causes either a cosmological bounce or turnaround; (c) Starts at the critical point P1 which later evolves to the non-standard singularity. For the n = 3 case, f0 > 0 only leads to the behavior described in 2(a) while the remaining cases are all possible for f0 < 0. Therefore, it is possible to realize a late-time accelerating behavior for appropriate parameter choices. E.5.5 Perspective on anisotropic cosmologies in teleparallel cosmology Within TG, realization of various cosmological behaviors with possible late-time isotropization has been observed. However, further investigations still need to be performed especially since the main attention has been on the background cosmological behavior. Resolving the H0 tension problem is extremely important for any future model of cosmology, however, an anisotropic cosmology has not yet been shown to be a realistic path in producing the necessary dynamics for this since it would lead to multiple expansion profiles in the different orientations. Meanwhile, only one TG extension, that of f(T) gravity, has been explored for anisotropic cosmology40. Additionally, due to the spin connection choice, only the BT-I anisotropic cosmology has been extensively explored. In light of the newly presented good tetrad-spin connection pairs (at least for the f(T, B) class), the remaining BT cosmologies may now be explored. All in all, a substantial amount of research still remains to be explored for anisotropic cosmologies. (F.10d) Appendix G Boltzmann equations analysis At the present time, the CMB dominates the constraints on the standard model of cosmology. This era of precision cosmology can be seen through plots of the current status of the power spectra 302 coming from the CMB. Furthermore, this spectrum carries relevant information on both the earlyand late-time Universe. We can take advantage of modified versions of the CLASS code41 to analyze the perturbations. This implementation allows the analysis of structure formation since each power spectrum is related to the curvature, baryonic matter, dark matter, etc. We start with the perturbations obtained for ΛCDM and afterwards we carry out a modified version that includes any modified/extended theory as an effective-like fluid. The effects will be seen as deviations in the power spectrum. These perturbations are described by equations for density contrast and velocity divergence in the synchronous gauge and valid for a perfect fluid (see Sec. 7 for examples on the procedure through which these perturbations are implemented) [1163, 1164] ˙δi + 3H(c 2 s,eff − wi) h δi + 3H(1 + wi) vi k i + (1 + ωi)kvi + 3Hw˙i vi k = −3(1 + wi)h , ˙ (G.1a) v˙i + H(1 − 3c 2 s,eff)vi = kδic 2 s,eff 1 + wi . (G.1b) The derivatives denoted by dots are wrt the conformal time, H is the conformal Hubble parameter, c 2 s,eff is the effective sound speed, vi is the velocity of the ith fluid, δi are the perturbations of each matter component, i.e baryons, photons, radiation, cold dark matter, and wi is the EoS for each component and k is the wave mode. One way to implement these equations of motion is through the Parameterized Post-Friedmann [1165] approach in the CLASS code, which is written in the programming language C and requires no specific version of the compiler; it has flexibility because it is not hard coded, it has a clear structure and a dynamical allocation of all indices. Furthermore, it controls accuracy as all accuracy parameters are grouped within a single structure; and finally it is faster than other codes. In order to work with CLASS, one has to express quantities and equations in terms of the specific code units. The units for the wavenumbers k and the Hubble parameter in the conformal time H are 1/Mpc, while the conformal time τ has the units of Mpc. Also, we employ the units from Sec. 1.3. Finally, the default CMB multipoles (Cl ’s) are dimensionless. A schematic architecture is depicted in Fig. 51 and the process to implement TG models is illustrated (with their equations) in the top left panels of Figs. 52–53. Appendix H Surveys and cosmological data The interest in understanding the physics of the late Universe can be well comprehended by using observational data from: SNeIa luminosity distances from the Pantheon compilation [871], BAO from redshift surveys [1166, 1167, 1168], and high-z measurements of H(z) from galaxy ages, the so-called Cosmic Chronometers (CC) [801]. To carry out cosmological tests on the free parameters that can be considered in the TG theories described in Sec. 10.3, we are going to consider the numerical solutions over theoretical parameters imposed by each model and determine the specific cosmological parameters for each model in addition to Ωm0 and H0. Publicly available Boltzmann codes, such as CLASS [1169], along with MCMC-like methods, as implemented in Monte Python [1170] can constrain the models using joint data sets, for instance, with CC + SNeIa + BAO. 306 The survey compilations considered for these studies described in this Review are provided in the following sections. H.1 Galaxy ages compilations Modified gravity constraints have been studied through measurements related to the galaxy ages. Currently, this kind of observable includes a sample of 51 observations in the redshift range 0.07 < z < 2.0 [801]. A calibration using stellar evolution from the BC03 model [1171] of this sample was presented in Ref. [1172] reducing this sample to 31 data points. The normalized parameter h(z) can be computed by considering the values from Planck 2018 and SH0ES+H0LiCOW. In this sample, 31 data points from passive galaxies are included, and 20 data points are estimated from BAO data under a ΛCDM prior. However, BAO data points can be computed by using the rs at the drag epoch (which is when photon pressure stops supporting gravitational instability in baryons and occurs slightly after the decoupling of photons) from PL18 . The free parameters of the cosmological model are determined through χ 2 -statistics through χ 2 H = #data X i=1 [H (zi , x) − Hobs(zi)]2 σ 2 H(zi) , (H.1) where Hobs(zi) is the observed value at zi , σH(zi) are the observational errors, and H (zi , x) is the value of a theoretical Hubble parameter H for the same zi with the specific parameter vector x. H.2 Pantheon type Ia supernovae compilation The distance modulus data can be added to the analysis as a late-time observable by considering its current sample denoted by the latest Type Ia SN compilations [871] and it contains 1048 SNeIa in the redshift range 0.01 < z < 2.26. In the below analyses, we also make use of the preceding SNLS-SDSS JLA [798], consisting of 740 SNeIa. The constraining power of this kind of SN sample is such that these observations can be used as standard candles. This can be implemented through the use of the distance modulus F(z, A)theo := 5 log10 [DL(z, A)] + µ0 . (H.2) The nuisance parameter µ0 encodes the Hubble parameter and the absolute magnitude M (which is a consatnt [1173]), and has to be marginalized over and DL(z, A) is the luminosity distance given by DL(z, A) := (1 + z) ˆ z 0 c dz 0 H(z 0 , A) , (H.3) and A = {w0, wa} is the vector with the free cosmological parameters to be fitted. We notice that the factor c/H0 can be rewritten in terms of µ0. This equation can be seen to contain the nuisance parameter µ0, which turns to be a function of the Hubble constant, the speed of light c, and the SNeIa absolute magnitude. This log-likelihood can also be expressed by marginalizing χ 2 SNeIa analytically wrt µ0, from which we obtain a new χ 2 SNeIa estimator χ 2 SNeIa(A) = (∆F(A))T C −1 SNeIa∆F(A) + ln S 2π − k 2 (A) S , (H.5) 307 where S = P ij C −1 SNeIaij is the sum of all the components of C −1 SNeIa. (H.6) For this sample we consider the nuisance parameter M inside the sample, which we can choose from a statistical analysis of the ΛCDM model with a fixed H0 from the late Universe measurements. H.3 Baryon acoustic oscillations compilation According to fluctuations in the density of the visible baryonic matter of the Universe, the BAO caused by acoustic density waves in the primordial plasma of the early Universe can be used as a tool to constrain cosmological parameters. Currently, their sample is characterized by a set of 15 transverse measurements which are obtained from the angular diameter distance in a quasi modelindependent approach. This can be done by computing the 2-point angular correlation function tracers via DA(z; rdrag) [1174]. The sample spans a redshift range 0.11 . z . 2.225. These kind of observations contribute to important features by comparing the data of the sound horizon at present, to the sound horizon at the time of recombination (extracted from the CMB anisotropy data). The BAO distances are given by dz ≡ rs(zd) DV (z) , with rs(zd) = c H0 ´ ∞ zd cs(z 0 ) E(z 0) dz 0 and rs(zd) being the comoving sound horizon at the baryon drag epoch, c the light velocity, zd is the drag epoch redshift and c 2 s = c 2/3[1 + (3Ωb0/4Ωγ0)(1 + z) −1 ] the sound speed, with Ωb0 and Ωγ0 the present values of baryon and photon energy density parameters, respectively. The dilation scale is given by DV (z, Ωm; A) =  c z(1 + z) 2D2 A H(z, Ωm; A) 1/3 , (H.7) where DA is the angular diameter distance DA(z, Ωm; A) = 1 1 + z ˆ z 0 c dz 0 H(z 0 , Ωm; A) , (H.8) where A = {w0, wa}. Through the comoving sound horizon, the distance ratio dz is related to the expansion parameter h (defined such that H(z) .= 100h(z)) and the physical densities Ωm and Ωb. H.5 H0 values As described in the introductory part of this section, there has been an decrease in the reported values of H0 coming from CMB data [372] using the ΛCDM model against model independent measurements of this parameter. We recall that the Planck Collaboration reported a low value of 67.4± 0.5 km s−1Mpc−1 [372] while the DES Collaboration gave a similar value of 67.4 +1.1 −1.2 km s−1Mpc−1 [1175]. Consequently, these predicted values of H0 contrast with the cosmology independent estimates from late-time observations, where the highest of these values is given by HR 0 = 74.22 ± 1.82 km s−1Mpc−1 [718]. Another late-time H0 value was reported by the H0LiCOW Collaboration [727] with a value of HHW 0 = 73.3 +1.7 −1.8 km s−1Mpc−1 . Another value was reported via the tip of the red giant branch method, which is one of the most accurate and precise means of measuring distances to 309 nearby galaxies, where HTRGB 0 = 69.8±1.9 km s−1Mpc−1 [1176]. Although this method has been used for over thirty years to infer high-precision distances to a large number of nearby galaxies, it is only recently that the TRGB method has been applied directly to the determination of H0 [1177, 737]. The χ 2 -statistic for any Hi 0 prior is given by χ 2 Hi 0 = H (z = 0, x) − Hi 0,obs2 σ 2 Hi 0 , (H.18) where Hi 0,obs denotes the observed value of H0 from the i th cosmic probe, σ 2 Hi 0 is the corresponding observational error, and H (z = 0, x) is the theoretical value of H0 with the specific model parameter vector x. Appendix I Bayesian recipe for cosmology Usually, it turns out to be very difficult to numerically compute the posterior distribution and the corresponding best-fits of the cosmological model parameters. For these non-standard setups, the available numerical tools play an important role during the parameter estimation task. There exists several options to carry out this work; nevertheless here we will focus only on MCMC with the Metropolis Hastings algorithm. The purpose of a Monte Carlo algorithm is to construct sequences of data points, which are the so-called chains, in a parameter space to evaluate a Bayesian posterior. A MCMC simulation can be assigned to certain algorithms that use random number generators to approximate a specific quantity. Moreover, a succession X1, X2, . . . , Xn of elements of a set composed by n elements, is a Monte Carlo set while the conditional distribution of Xn+1 given X1, . . . , Xn depends solely on Xn, i.e., a MCMC is a process where we can compute subsequent steps based on the information given by the previous data points. A relevant property of a MCMC is that it converges to a stationary scenario where successive elements of the chain are samples from the distribution; therefore it converges to the posterior P(θ|D, H), where θ are the free cosmological parameters of the model, D is the data and H the hypothesised model. In this way, we can estimate the standard quantities of interest. The number of points required to obtain better estimates in MCMC tends to scale linearly with the number of parameters of the model, so that, this method becomes much faster as the dimensionality increases. The density is approximated by a set of delta functions given by p(θ|D, H) ' 1 N X N i=1 δ(θ − θi), (I.1) where Θi denotes the observable data and with N being the number of points in the chain. The posterior mean can be calculated using hθi = ˆ θP(θ, H|D)dθ ' 1 N X N i=1 θi , (I.2) where the integral intervals can be assumed to be as [a, b], which can be divided into n equally spaced points depending on the observational sample and size of the nested, and where ' is used since the samples θi are generated out of the posterior by numerical construction. Then, we can estimate any integrals using Simpson’s rule as hf(θ)i = ˆ f(θ)P(f(θ), H|D)df(θ) ' 1 N X N i=1 f(θi). (I.3) In a MCMC routine it is necessary to generate a new point θi+1 from the previous point θi . However, as expected, we need a criterion for accepting (or refusing) this new point, depending on whether it 310 turns out to fit the data better for our model or not. If this new step is worse than the previous one, we may accept it with a certain probability, since it could be the case that, if we only accept steps with better probability, we could be converging into a local maximum in our parameter space and, therefore, not completely mapping all of the points. The standard adopted algorithm that contains this information is the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. In this kind of algorithm it is necessary to start from a random pivot point θi , with an associated posterior probability pi = p(θi |D, H). Afterwards, we need to propose a candidate variable θc from a proposed distribution q(θi , θc) used as a generator of new random points in the sequence. Then, the probability of accepting the new point can be defined by p(acceptance) := min  1, pcq(θc, θi) piq(θi , θc)  . (I.4) With a symmetric proposed distribution the algorithm reduces to the Metropolis algorithm p(acceptance) = min  1, pc pi  . (I.5) The full algorithm can therefore be detailed using the following steps: 1. Choose a random initial condition θi in the parameter space and compute the posterior distribution using Eq. (I.4). 2. Generate a new candidate from a proposal distribution in the parameter space and compute the corresponding posterior distribution using Eq. (I.5). 3. Accept (or not) the new point with the help of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm using Eq. (I.4). 4. If the point is not accepted, repeat the previous point in the chain. 5. Repeat steps 2–4 until you have a large enough chain (according to the Gelman–Rubin criteria). A schematic of this process is shown in Supplementary 3. Once the cosmological model is established, we need a statistical code to estimate the free parameters of our model. Fortunately there are several publicly available MCMC codes that can make this task easy to handle. In this Review and in the literature the Monte Python code is employed, which is a MCMC code for cosmological parameter extraction [1178]. This code contain likelihoods of the most recent cosmological experiments, and interfaces with the Boltzmann code Cosmic Linear Anisotropy Solving System (CLASS) [1179] observables. The code has several sampling methods available: Metropolis-Hastings, Nested Sampling (through MultiNest), EMCEE (through CosmoHammer) and Importance Sampling. To adapt our theories to the code, we must consider Gaussian likelihoods for each data compilation with the following form L ∝ exp " − X i (F(zi) − Fi) 2 2σi # , (I.6) where F(zi) is the theoretical value related to the observation Fi , and σi are the corresponding errors associated to each measurement. In our estimation F(zi) is given by the definitions of χ 2 (see Supplementary 4) for each cosmological observable. This function contains the background evolution and equation of state equations described for the TG theories. Appendix J Gaussian processes for cosmology Gaussian processes (GP) generalize the concept of a Gaussian distribution for a finite set of data points to a continuous distribution over a specified range for a function (see Refs. [1180, 1181] for a comprehensive review on the topic). Thus, given a set of Gaussian distributed data points, GP 311 provide an iterative process by which to produce the most likely underlying continuous function that describes the data together with its associated confidence bounds without assuming a prescribed form of the function [1182]. In the current era of precision cosmology with multiple state-of-the-art surveys, GP has been exhaustively applied in cosmology [1183, 1182, 1184, 1185, 1186, 1187, 1188, 1189, 1190, 1191, 1192, 1193, 1194, 1195, 1196, 594, 1197, 1198], particularly to infer the late-time dynamics of the Universe. As previously mentioned, GP extends the idea of a Gaussian distribution by defining a mean function µ(z) together with a two-point covariance function C(z, z0 ) to form a GP as a continuous curve ξ(z) ∼ GP (µ(z), C(z, z0 )) , (J.1) together with its associated error regions ∆ξ(z), thus resulting in ξ(z) ± ∆ξ(z). Here, z 0 represents other points in the training data set. Without losing generality, the mean can be set to zero for all points in the reconstruction, since each point is not very sensitive to this. For the redshifts z ∗ of the reconstruction at which we do not have data points, we can define a kernel function for the covariance such that C z ∗ , z∗ 0 = K z ∗ , z∗ 0 , which will produce the reconstruction at those points. The kernel will embody all the information about the strength of the correlations between these reconstructed values as well as the amplitude of the deviations from the mean [1190]. The only generic property about this is that it must be a symmetric function. On the other hand, for observational data points z˜ where observations exist, we have access to the associated errors and covariance matrix D (˜z, z˜ 0 ) between the points, so that the covariance can be written as C (˜z, z˜ 0 ) = K (˜z, z˜ 0 ) + D (˜z, z˜ 0 ) which will give information about the kernel. Lastly, observational points and reconstructed points will be correlated by the kernel alone through C (z ∗ , z˜ 0 ) = K (z ∗ , z˜ 0 ) [1199]. There exists a number of kernel function choices [1181], where some behave slightly better in certain situations, which remains an open discussion in the literature [1182]. In this Review, we will only be considering the square exponential kernel function, specified by K (z, z˜) = σ 2 f exp " − (z − z˜) 2 2l 2 f # , (J.2) where σf and lf are the kernel hyperparameters which relate the strength and scope of the correlations between the reconstructed data points, respectively [1200]. Here, the hyperparameters are statistical parameters rather than model parameters. In this setting, hyperparameters model the functional behaviour of the underlying data points without any knowledge of the physical processes being undertaken. The hyperparameter lf can be considered as the typical correlation length scale of the independent variable, while the signal variance σf , can be thought of as the typical variation scale of the dependent variable. The observational data being input into a GP then appears as a subset of Gaussian points that can be extended through the GP approach. This is achieved by maximizing the likelihood of the GP producing the observational data by estimating the underlying functional behavior for different values of the hyperparameters for particular kernel instances. Furthermore, the GP approach is model-independent in the context of a physical model and instead assumes a particular statistical kernel which dictates the correlation between the reconstructed points. The GP approach is also non-parametric in terms of physical models. For a Gaussian prior for both the data and the random functions, one can marginalize over the space of functions and obtain the logarithm of the marginal likelihood via a Bayesian approach ln L = − 1 2 X N i,j=1  [yi − µ(xi)] [K(xi , xj ) + C(xi , xj )]−1 [yj − µ(xj )] − 1 2 ln |K(xi , xj ) + C(xi , xj )| − N 2 ln 2π . (J.3) The optimal hyperparameter values of σf and lf are then inferred via the maximisation of the logarithm of the marginal likelihood. 312 This reconstruction method can also be implemented for the reconstruction of the derivatives of a function which has been GP reconstructed, since the derivatives will again be a GP. The discussed GP algorithm is nicely implemented in a publicly available Python code GaPP (GP in Python) [1201, 1200], which reconstructs a continuous function for any given data set along with its derivative functions. Appendix K Machine learning for cosmology Bayesian methods remain the preferred choice compared to the information criterion and GP reported in the literature [1202]. A complete Bayesian method for model selection is highly involved computationally and usually suffers from multi modal posteriors and free parameter degeneracies. The calculation of the required evidence, in order to obtain a final result, is an immensely time consuming process which makes it very expensive computationally. The study of LSS necessitates the use of computer simulations in order to address the issue of constraining cosmological parameters using Bayesian methods. Due to the computational complexity of these simulations, some studies remain computationally unfeasible for the foreseeable future. It is at this point that computational techniques such as machine learning can have a number of important uses, even as for example for trying to understand the evolution of our Universe. On the issue of LSS, on a macroscopic level, galactic structure form clusters which are some of the largest known objects to populate the Universe. On even larger scales, filamentary structures are observed which are composed of galactic superclusters that are billions of light years in term of their length scale. This is the LSS of the Universe, and by measuring its properties and structure, we can test different cosmological models of the evolution of the Universe. These structures are often described by a matter density field, or by its statistical properties through the matter power spectrum. These can be measured in a variety of ways: CMB photons travel through the LSS and thus interacts with it. This leaves an imprint on the photon properties which is then used to infer the structure and growth of the LSS. Large-scale galaxy surveys and intensity mapping experiments directly sample the matter density field, allowing us to build up an image of the LSS with unparalleled precision. Surveys of galaxy clusters—whether from optical surveys, X-ray, or through their Sunyaev-Zeldovich interaction with the CMB—sample the extreme peaks of the density field. Sampling the LSS through its greatest non-linearities gives a powerful lever arm on the physics that drive its evolution. The scheme behind the machine learning is based on considering a neural network with a complex combination of several neurons organised in nested layers. Each of these neuron implements a function that is parametrized by a set of weights which can be denoted by W. Each layer of a neural network thus transforms one input vector - or tensor depending the dimension of the system - to another through a differentiable function. Theoretically, given a neuron n that has an input vector and the choice of an activation function An, the output of the neuron can be calculated as h = An(h · Wh + x · Wx + ba), (K.1a) y t = An(h t · Wy + by), (K.1b) where b is the bias, h is called the hidden state, An is the activation function, x is the input data and y t is the output. We introduce a data set in order to train this array and therefore the architecture can learn to finally give an output set of data. For example: the network can learn the distribution of the distance moduli in the DE models, then feed the astrophysical samplers (surveys) to the network to reconstruct the DE model and then discriminate the most probable model42. Interesting works in that these directions have been developed in Ref. [792, 791]. While neural networks can learn complex nested representations of the data sample, allowing them to achieve high performance levels, it also bounds our understanding of the model learned by 42In this text review we are employing a recurrence neural network. There are several approaches in this machine learning field e.g. in Ref. [1203] and references therein. 313 Figure 55: A deep learning architecture for a cosmological model. On the left we have an example of an observed data as an input, on the middle the architecture of an optimal deep neural network and finally, as output results, on the right the cosmological parameters that describe the cosmological model. Permission for use of this figure was kindly provided by the authors of Ref. [1202]. the network itself. The choice of an architecture [1203] can have an important relevant influence on the performance of the neural network. Some methods have to be designed by evaluating the number and type of layers, and the number and the size of the filters used per layer. A good way to select these choices is through experimentation, which we can do since we have different data sets from observational cosmology. We can select the size of the network, which depends on the number of training tests, because networks with a large number of cosmological parameters are likely to be over-fitted if not enough training tests are available. A growing interest in these kind of algorithms has put forward new opportunities for data-driven cosmological analyses, but also the adoption of machine learning approaches also opens new challenges for the community. In our case, we consider deep learning, a method that can interpret the results when the data are highly complex for standard model developments. A number of proposals in this area have been suggested to explore the deep learning methods for measurements of cosmological parameters from density fields [1204] and for future large-scale photometric surveys [1205]. To start to train an astrophysical or a cosmological sample, we need to design an architecture with a function of neural network, that can have many unstable points and a local minima. This architecture makes the optimisation process very difficult, but in real scenarios, high levels of noise degrade the training data and results in optimisation scenarios with more local minima points and increases the difficulty in training the neural network. It is desirable to start by optimising the neural network using noise-free data which typically yield smoother scenarios. As an example, in Fig. 55 we present a standard network using an image of a cosmological simulation (the data) and then we divided an array of several layers to finally, extract the output cosmological parameters value. Each neuron uses a Bayesian process to compute the error propagation as it is done in the standard inference analyses. We can describe a brief but effective recipe to develop a recurrence neural network with a Bayesian computation training in the following steps: • Step 1 - Design of the the neural network – For a recurrence neural network method we can select values that have one layer and a specific number of neurons. • Step 2 - Organising the data sample – We need to sort the samples from lower to higher redshift z in the observations. Afterwards, we can re-arrange our data using a number of steps that compares the same points of the data samples, e.g. if a SN sample contains approximately 1000 data points, then our array should be of the same dimension of the data sample. • Step 3 - Bayesian training – It is important to choose a model of regularization. With 314 a Bayesian standard method to calculate the evidence, the algorithm can calculate errors via regularization methods. Finally, over the cost function we can use Adam optimiser. • Step 4 - Training the full architecture – It is required to consider a high number of epochs (e.g for a sampler as Pantheon SN, one can use around 1000 epoch per layer). After the training, we need to read the model, which now will be the new initial model and apply the architecture using the same hyperparameters and re-run the algorithm until we got the final convergence. The result of this step is the construction of the confidence regions. • Step 5 - Calculation of the modulus distance µ(z) for each cosmological model – Using H(z), we can compute µ(z) by using a specific dark energy EoS in terms of z and then integrate them. • Step 6 - Calculations of best-fits – The output values can be obtained by using the training data as a simulated sample. For this case we use the publicly codes CLASS and Monte Python to constrain the models as it is standard as it is done in the standard Bayesian cosmology case.
